issues.legal_issue: A consumer complaint seeking compensation for recurring financial injury caused by a promoter’s continuing failure to obtain an occupancy certificate is not barred by limitation while that failure continues.
material_facts: The promoter had an obligation under the governing law and the sale arrangements to obtain an occupancy certificate.
The promoter did not obtain the certificate, including after a consumer forum ordered it to do so.
Because the certificate remained unavailable, the municipal authorities repeatedly charged the society’s members higher property taxes and water charges.
The society filed a consumer complaint seeking reimbursement of the additional charges and was pursuing execution of the earlier order concerning the certificate.
issues.conclusion: The promoter’s continuing failure to obtain the occupancy certificate was a continuing wrong causing repeated injury, so the complaint seeking compensation for its consequences was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24A of the Consumer Protection Act 1986 generally requires a complaint to be filed within two years of the cause of action. Section 22 of the Limitation Act 1963 provides for a fresh limitation period during each moment of a continuing breach of contract or tort. Under Balakrishna Savalram Pujari Waghmare v. Shree Dhyaneshwar Maharaj Sansthan, a continuing wrong requires continuing injury from the wrongful act, not merely continuing effects of a completed injury. CWT v. Suresh Seth explains that a continuing wrong may arise from repeated acts or omissions or breach of a duty that requires continuing performance. M. Siddiq v. Suresh Das confirms that a continuing wrong requires breach of a continuing duty. Here, the promoter’s continuing duty to obtain the certificate was breached, and the resulting higher charges were repeatedly imposed.

rule.if: consumer_complaint and promoter_has_continuing_certificate_duty and certificate_remains_unobtained and higher_charges_recur

predicates.consumer_complaint: A claimant filed a complaint before a consumer forum seeking compensation for harm attributed to a service provider.
predicates.promoter_has_continuing_certificate_duty: A promoter remained obliged under the applicable arrangements or law to obtain an occupancy certificate for the purchasers or their association.
predicates.certificate_remains_unobtained: The promoter failed to obtain the occupancy certificate, including after being directed to do so.
predicates.higher_charges_recur: The absence of the certificate led authorities to impose higher charges repeatedly on the purchasers or their association.

issues.definition: When a consumer complaint is based on a promoter’s continuing failure to obtain a required certificate that repeatedly causes higher charges, the complaint is not barred by limitation.

issues.legal_issue: Purchasers may maintain a consumer claim against a promoter for compensation for additional charges imposed by public authorities when the promoter’s failure to obtain an occupancy certificate constitutes deficient service.
material_facts: The promoter was responsible for transferring the flats with an occupancy certificate.
The promoter failed to obtain the certificate.
The absence of the certificate resulted in the society’s members paying higher property taxes and water charges to municipal authorities.
The society sought compensation from the promoter for those additional charges.
issues.conclusion: The failure to obtain the occupancy certificate was a deficiency in service, and the purchasers could seek compensation as consumers for the resulting additional charges; the complaint was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(1)(d) and 2(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act 1986 define a consumer by reference to services availed for consideration and define deficiency as a shortcoming or inadequacy in service required by law. Wing Commander Arifur Rahman Khan v. DLF Southern Homes and Pioneer Urban Land Infrastructure v. Govindan Raghavan recognize that failure to obtain an occupancy certificate or comply with contractual obligations can amount to deficiency in service. Treaty Construction v. Ruby Tower Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. declined damages where there was no cogent basis to establish liability or assess loss; it did not prevent a claim where the failure and consequential liability were sufficiently established. The promoter’s liability arose from its own service obligation, even though the higher charges were collected by municipal authorities.

rule.if: consumer_complaint and promoter_service_included_certificate_obligation and promoter_failed_to_obtain_certificate and failure_caused_purchaser_expense

predicates.consumer_complaint: A claimant filed a complaint before a consumer forum seeking redress for an alleged deficiency in service.
predicates.promoter_service_included_certificate_ob: The promoter’s service or contractual undertaking to purchasers included providing or obtaining an occupancy certificate.
predicates.promoter_failed_to_obtain_certificate: The promoter did not obtain the occupancy certificate required for the purchasers or their association.
predicates.failure_caused_purchaser_expense: The absence of the certificate caused purchasers to incur additional charges or expenses imposed by another authority.

issues.definition: When a promoter fails to provide a certificate included in its service obligations and that failure causes purchasers additional expenses, the purchasers may maintain a consumer claim for compensation.
